arXiv:2011.03472v3 [math.AG] 01 Feb 2021

A note on the Jacobian ConjectureThanks: The author is partially supported by by the grant of Narodowe Centrum Nauki number 2019/33/B/ST1/00755.

Zbigniew Jelonek Address: Instytut Matematyczny PAN,
Śniadeckich 8, 00-656 Warszawa, Poland Email address: zjelonek@impan.gov.pl
Abstract.

Let F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a polynomial mapping with a non vanishing Jacobian. If the set SFS_{F} of non-properness of FF is smooth, then FF is a surjective mapping. Moreover, if SFS_{F} is connected, then χ⁡(SF)>0.\chi(S_{F})>0. Additionally, if n=2n=2, then the set SFS_{F} of non-properness of FF cannot be a curve without self-intersections.

Key words and phrases: 
etale morphisms, topological covering, jacobian conjecture
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14R15

1. Introduction

Let F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a generically finite polynomial mapping. The measure of the non-properness of FF is the set SF={y∈ℂn:thereisasequencexn→∞:F(xn)→y}S_{F}=\{y\in\mathbb{C}^{n}:\ there\ is\ a\ sequence\ x_{n}\to\infty:F(x_{n})\to y\}, which was introduced by the author in [5], [7]. This set if non-empty is a ℂ−\mathbb{C}-uniruled hypersurface (see [5], [7]). If FF is an etale mapping (as in the Jacobian Conjecture), then SF={y∈ℂn:#​f−1​(y)<μ⁡(F)},S_{F}=\{y\in\mathbb{C}^{n}:\#f^{-1}(y)<\mu(F)\}, where μ⁡(F)\mu(F) denotes the number of points in a general fiber of F.F. In particular, in this case the mapping FF is a topological covering over ℂn∖SF.\mathbb{C}^{n}\setminus S_{F}. In order to to prove the Jacobian Conjecture, it is enough to show that SF=∅.S_{F}=\emptyset. As the first step in this direction Nollet, Taylor and Xavier have proved in [9] that the set SFS_{F} cannot be a connected non-bifurcated algebraic hypersurface. More generally Nollet and Xavier have proved in [10] that the group π1​(ℂn∖SF)\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{n}\setminus S_{F}) cannot be abelian. Since there exist smooth connected hypersurfaces VV in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with non-abelian fundamental group π1​(ℂn∖V)\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{n}\setminus V) the following conjecture is still open (see [10]):

Conjecture. Let F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a polynomial mapping with a non vanishing Jacobian. Then the set SFS_{F} of non-properness of FF cannot be a smooth connected hypersurface.

This conjecture is true in dimension n=2.n=2. Indeed, in this case SFS_{F} has to be a parametric curve (see [7]), consequently it is isomorphic to ℂ.\mathbb{C}. But it is well known that such a curve is non-bifurcated (see [1], [12]) and by [9] conjecture is true in this dimension. Here we generalize the latter result and we prove:

Theorem 1.1.

Let F:ℂ2→ℂ2F:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2} be a polynomial mapping with a non vanishing Jacobian. Then the set SFS_{F} of non-properness of FF cannot be a curve without self-intersections.

Note that this is not true in the real case. In fact Pinchuk have constructed an example of a polynomial mapping F:ℝ2→ℝ2F:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2} with a non-vanishing Jacobian, for which the set of non-properness is a semi-algebraic curve homeomorphic to ℝ\mathbb{R} (see [11], [2], [3]). We finish giving a partial answer to the Conjecture above:

Theorem 1.2.

Let F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a polynomial mapping with a non vanishing Jacobian. Assume that the set SFS_{F} of non-properness of FF is smooth. Then FF is a surjective mapping. Moreover, if SFS_{F} is connected, then χ⁡(SF)>0.\chi(S_{F})>0.

2. Proof of Theorem 1.1

In the sequel we need the topological characterization of an irreducible algebraic curve with Euler characteristic 11 will be useful. Let us begin with the following simple observation (see e.g. [6]). The Euler characteristic of the set XX we will denote by χ⁡(X).\chi(X).

Theorem 2.1.

Let XX be an irreducible affine curve of genus gg. (It means that a smooth model X1X_{1} of a compactification of XX has genus gg.) Let us suppose that XX has nn points at infinity (i.e., nn is the number of points in X1∖X0X_{1}\setminus X_{0}, where X0X_{0} is the normalization of XX). Let S​i​n​g​(X)={a1,…,ar}Sing(X)=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}\} be the singular locus. Further suppose that the germ XaiX_{a_{i}} has kik_{i} irreducible components. Then

χ⁡(X)=2​(1−g)−n−∑i=1r(ki−1).\chi(X)=2(1-g)-n-\sum_{i=1}^{r}(k_{i}-1).
Corollary 2.2.

Let XX be an irreducible affine curve. Then χ⁡(X)≤1\chi(X)\leq 1 and the equality holds if and only if XX is homeomorphic to ℂ.\mathbb{C}.

Plane curves homeomorphic to the complex line have a very nice description due to Zaidenberg and Lin (see [8]):

Theorem 2.3.

Let X⊂ℂ2X\subset{\hbox{\tenmsy C}}^{2} be an affine algebraic curve homeomorphic to a complex line. Then in suitable coordinates XX may be written as

X={(x,y)∈ℂ2:xk=yl,(k,l)=1}.X=\{(x,y)\in{\hbox{\tenmsy C}}^{2}:x^{k}=y^{l},\ \ (k,l)=1\}.

For plane curves isomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} we have the famous Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki theorem (see [1], [12]):

Theorem 2.4.

If Γ⊂ℂ2\Gamma\subset\hbox{\tenmsy C}^{2} is a curve isomorphic to ℂ then in some coordinates we have Γ={(x,y)∈ℂ2:x=0}.\Gamma=\{(x,y)\in\hbox{\tenmsy C}^{2}:x=0\}.

The following proposition was proved in [13] and is important in our study:

Theorem 2.5.

Let f:ℂ2⟶ℂf:{\hbox{\tenmsy C}}^{2}\longrightarrow{\hbox{\tenmsy C}} be a primitive polynomial and let χp\chi_{p} denote the Euler characteristic of a general fiber. Let SS denote a set of all singular points. For every s∈Ss\in S we have χ⁡(Γs)>χp\chi(\Gamma_{s})>\chi_{p}. Moreover

∑s∈S{χ⁡(Γs)−χp}=1−χp.\sum_{s\in S}\{\chi(\Gamma_{s})-\chi_{p}\}=1-\chi_{p}.

We get at once the following interesting:

Corollary 2.6.

If a singular fiber Γs\Gamma_{s} of a family ff has Euler characteristic one, then all other fibers of ff has not characteristic one.

Proof.

Indeed from Theorem 2.5 we have that Γs\Gamma_{s} is the unique atypical fiber. If any other fiber has Euler characteristic one, then, since it is general it has to be isomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} and by Theorem 2.4 all fibers are isomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} and ff has not a singular fiber- a contradiction. ∎

Finally we need the following nice result of Gwoździewicz (see [4]):

Theorem 2.7.

Let F:ℂ2→ℂ2F:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2} be a polynomial mapping with a non vanishing Jacobian. Assume that FF is injective on some line L⊂ℂ.L\subset\mathbb{C}. Then FF is an isomorphism.

Now we pass to the proof of Theorem 1.1. Let F:ℂ2→ℂ2F:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2} be a polynomial mapping with a non vanishing Jacobian and assume that the set SFS_{F} of non-properness of FF is a curve without self-intersections. First we show that the curve SFS_{F} is irreducible. Assume that SFS_{F} has at least two components AA and B.B. By [7] the curves A,BA,B have polynomial parametrizations. In particular their normalization are isomorphic to ℂ.\mathbb{C}. Since SFS_{F} has not self-intersection we see that A,BA,B are homeomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} and consequently they have Euler characteristic equal to one.

Let hAh_{A}, hBh_{B} be irreducible equation of AA and B.B. We can asuume deg hA≥h_{A}\geq deg hB.h_{B}. Consider hBh_{B} as a regular function on A.A. Since AA and BB have not common points, the function hBh_{B} is non-zero on A.A. But AA is a parametric curve (see [7]), hence the function hBh_{B} restricted to AA has to be a constant c.c. In particular hAh_{A} divides hB−ch_{B}-c and since deg hA≥h_{A}\geq deg hBh_{B} we have hA=k⁡(hB−c),h_{A}=k(h_{B}-c), where k∈ℂ∗.k\in\mathbb{C}^{*}. Consequently BB is a fiber in the family given by ha=t.h_{a}=t. If AA or BB is a singular curve, then by Corollary 2.6 we get a contradiction. If AA is smooth then also BB and all other components of SFS_{F} are smooth by Theorem 2.4. In particular in some system of coordinates we have SF={(x,y)∈ℂ2:∏i=1r(x−ai)=0}.S_{F}=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}:\prod^{r}_{i=1}(x-a_{i})=0\}. Take t∉{a1,…,ar}.t\not\in\{a_{1},...,a_{r}\}. Let LL be a line {x=t}.\{x=t\}. The mapping FF is proper over LL, hence the restriction F−1​(L)∋x↦F⁡(x)∈LF^{-1}(L)\ni x\mapsto F(x)\in L is a topological covering. If L′L^{\prime} is an irreducible component of F−1​(L)F^{-1}(L) then the mapping F|L′F|_{L^{\prime}} is an isomorphism, in particular L′L^{\prime} is isomorphic to ℂ.\mathbb{C}. By Theorem 2.4 we can assume that the curve L′L^{\prime} is a line in ℂ2.\mathbb{C}^{2}. Since the mapping F|L′F|_{L^{\prime}} is injective, by Theorem 2.7 we see that the mapping FF is an isomorphism, consequently SF=∅S_{F}=\emptyset, which is a contradiction.

Thus we can assume that SFS_{F} is an irreducible curve and it is homeomorphic to ℂ.\mathbb{C}. In particular χ⁡(SF)=1.\chi(S_{F})=1. Take U=ℂ2∖SF.U=\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus S_{F}. We have χ⁡(U)=χ⁡(ℂ2∖SF)=χ⁡(ℂ2)−χ⁡(SF)=1−1=0.\chi(U)=\chi(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus S_{F})=\chi(\mathbb{C}^{2})-\chi(S_{F})=1-1=0. Take U′=F−1​(U).U^{\prime}=F^{-1}(U). Since SF∩U=∅S_{F}\cap U=\emptyset, we see that the mapping F:U′→UF:U^{\prime}\to U is proper, in particular this mapping is a topological covering of degree d=μ⁡(F)d=\mu(F) (here μ⁡(F)\mu(F) is a geometric degree of FF). In particular χ⁡(U′)=d​χ​(U)=0.\chi(U^{\prime})=d\chi(U)=0. Note that F−1​(SF)=ℂ2∖U′F^{-1}(S_{F})=\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus U^{\prime}. Hence χ⁡(F−1​(SF))=χ⁡(ℂ2)−χ⁡(U′)=1−0=1.\chi(F^{-1}(S_{F}))=\chi(\mathbb{C}^{2})-\chi(U^{\prime})=1-0=1. Let F−1​(SF)=⋃i=1rAiF^{-1}(S_{F})=\bigcup^{r}_{i=1}A_{i} be the decomposition of F−1​(SF)F^{-1}(S_{F}) into irreducible components. Of course Ai∩Aj=∅A_{i}\cap A_{j}=\emptyset for i≠ji\not=j and consequently χ⁡(⋃i=1rAi)=∑i=1rχ⁡(Ai).\chi(\bigcup^{r}_{i=1}A_{i})=\sum^{r}_{i=1}\chi(A_{i}). By Corollary 2.2 we see that there exists AiA_{i} such that χ⁡(Ai)=1.\chi(A_{i})=1. In particular AiA_{i} is homeomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} and consequently it has only one place at infinity. Thus the mapping g=F|Ai:Ai→SFg=F|_{A_{i}}:A_{i}\to S_{F} is proper, hence it is a topological covering. Since SFS_{F} is homeomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} this mapping is in fact a homeomorphism. Using Theorem 2.3 we can assume that the curve SFS_{F} is given by the equation xp=yqx^{p}=y^{q}, where (p,q)=1.(p,q)=1. Denote O=(0,0).O=(0,0). Let O′=g−1​(O)O^{\prime}=g^{-1}(O) and let LL be the line {x=0}\{x=0\}. Note that L∩SF={O}.L\cap S_{F}=\{O\}. Denote by L′L^{\prime} this component of the curve F−1​(L)F^{-1}(L) which contains the point O′O^{\prime} and let h=F|L′.h=F|_{L^{\prime}}.

We will compute χ⁡(L′).\chi(L^{\prime}). If V=L∖{O}V=L\setminus\{O\}, then the mapping h:h−1​(V):=V′→Vh:h^{-1}(V):=V^{\prime}\to V is proper, hence a topological covering. Since χ⁡(V)=χ⁡(L∖{O})=χ⁡(L)−χ⁡({O})=1−1=0\chi(V)=\chi(L\setminus\{O\})=\chi(L)-\chi(\{O\})=1-1=0, we have as before that χ​(h−1​(V))=0.\chi(h^{-1}(V))=0. In particular χ⁡(L′)≥χ⁡(V′)+χ⁡(O′)=1\chi(L^{\prime})\geq\chi(V^{\prime})+\chi(O^{\prime})=1. Consequently by Corollary 2.2 we have χ⁡(L′)=1.\chi(L^{\prime})=1. Since the curve L′L^{\prime} is smooth we see that it is isomorphic to ℂ.\mathbb{C}. Since the curve L′L^{\prime} has only one place at infinity the mapping h:L′→Lh:L^{\prime}\to L is proper and of course it has not ramifications. Hence it is an isomorphism. By Theorem 2.4 we can assume that the curve L′L^{\prime} is a line in ℂ2.\mathbb{C}^{2}. Since the mapping F|L′F|_{L^{\prime}} is injective, by Theorem 2.7 we see that the mapping FF is an isomorphism, consequently SF=∅S_{F}=\emptyset, which is a contradiction.

3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

We start with:

Theorem 3.1.

Let (V,a)⊂(ℂN,a)(V,a)\subset(\mathbb{C}^{N},a) be a germ of n−n-dimensional normal variety. Assume that F:(Va,a)→(ℂn,0)F:(V_{a},a)\to(\mathbb{C}^{n},0) is a proper holomorphic mapping with the critical set CC and the discriminant D=F⁡(C¯).D=F(\overline{C}). If DD is smooth, then VaV_{a} is a smooth germ and there is an integer rr such that in some coordinates we have

F:Va∋(x1,x2,…,xn)↦(x1r,x2,…,xn).F:V_{a}\ni(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\mapsto(x_{1}^{r},x_{2},...,x_{n}).
Proof.

Take so small ball B⁡(0,r):=BB(0,r):=B such that in some coordinates we have D={x∈B:x1=0}.D=\{x\in B:x_{1}=0\}. We can assume that the mapping F:V→BF:V\to B is well defined and proper. In particular the mapping F:V∖F−1​(D)→B∖DF:V\setminus F^{-1}(D)\to B\setminus D is a topological covering. Since π1​(B∖D)=ℤ\pi_{1}(B\setminus D)=\mathbb{Z} we have F∗​(π1​(V∖F−1​(D))=(r)⊂ℤCLOSE,F_{*}(\pi_{1}(V\setminus F^{-1}(D))=(r)\subset\mathbb{Z}, where rr is a natural number. Let g:ℂn∋(x1,x2,…,xn)↦(x1r,x2,…,xn)∈ℂng:\mathbb{C}^{n}\ni(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\mapsto(x_{1}^{r},x_{2},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{C}^{n} and take B′=g−1​(B).B^{\prime}=g^{-1}(B). Take g:B′∖{x:x1=0}∋x↦π⁡(x)∈B∖D.g:B^{\prime}\setminus\{x:x_{1}=0\}\ni x\mapsto\pi(x)\in B\setminus D.

We show that F:V→BF:V\to B is holomorphically equivalent to g:B′→B.g:B^{\prime}\to B. Since F∗​(π1​(V∖F−1​(D)))=g∗​(π1​(B′∖{x:x1=0})=(r)CLOSEF_{*}(\pi_{1}(V\setminus F^{-1}(D)))=g_{*}(\pi_{1}(B^{\prime}\setminus\{x:x_{1}=0\})=(r) we can lift the covering FF to a holomorphic mapping ϕ:→Pfi\phi:\to P_{f_{i}} such that following diagram commutes:

Since the mappings FF and gg are proper, the mapping ϕ\phi is locally bounded and by the Riemann extension theorem it can be extended to a holomorphic mapping Φ\Phi on the whole of B′.B^{\prime}. Since VV is normal we can also extend the mapping ϕ−1\phi^{-1} to a holomorphic mapping Ψ:V→B′.\Psi:V\to B^{\prime}. Since ψ∘ϕ=i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y\psi\circ\phi=identity we have also Ψ∘Φ=i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y\Psi\circ\Phi=identity. In particular VV is amooth at a.a. ∎

Corollary 3.2.

Under assumptions above we have F−1​(D)=C.F^{-1}(D)=C.

Now we can prove Theorem 1.2. By the Zariski Main Theorem in version of Grothendieck there exists a normal variety VV and a finite mapping F¯:V→ℂn\overline{F}:V\to\mathbb{C}^{n} such that

a) ℂn⊂V,\mathbb{C}^{n}\subset V,

b) F¯|ℂn=F.\overline{F}|_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}=F.

Take S=SFS=S_{F} and let T=F−1​(S).T=F^{-1}(S). Since the mapping FF is quasi-finite, the set F⁡(T)F(T) is dense in S.S. It is enough to prove that TT is closed in VV and then the mapping F:T→SF:T\to S is finite and hence surjective. Assume that TT is not closed and let a∈T¯∩(V∖ℂn).a\in\overline{T}\cap(V\setminus\mathbb{C}^{n}). Let b=F¯​(a).b=\overline{F}(a). Consider the mapping F¯:(V,a)→(ℂn,b).\overline{F}:(V,a)\to(\mathbb{C}^{n},b). It is easy to see that the discriminant of this mapping is 𝕊b{\hbox{\tenmsy S}}_{b} and it is smooth by the assumption. Hence by Theorem 3.1 we have that the germ 𝕃a:=(V∖ℂn)a\hbox{\tenmsy L}_{a}:=(V\setminus\mathbb{C}^{n})_{a} is a germ of smooth hypersurface and F¯−1​(𝕊b)=𝕃a.\overline{F}^{-1}({\hbox{\tenmsy S}}_{b})={\hbox{\tenmsy L}}_{a}. But 𝕋a⊂F¯−1​(𝕊b).{\hbox{\tenmsy T}}_{a}\subset\overline{F}^{-1}({\hbox{\tenmsy S}}_{b}). It is a contradiction.

Now assume that SS is connected and let a=χ⁡(S).a=\chi(S). Let qq be a topological degree of F.F. Since FF is not proper we have q>1.q>1. Outside SS the mapping FF is a topological covering of degree qq hence we have:

χ⁡(ℂn)=1=(1−a)​q+s​a=q−a⁡(q−s),\chi(\mathbb{C}^{n})=1=(1-a)q+sa=q-a(q-s),

where ss is a topological degree of a covering T→S.T\to S. Note that q−s>0.q-s>0. Hence if a<0a<0 we have 1>q1>q which is a contradiction. If a=0a=0 we have q=1q=1, consequently FF is an diffeomorphism and SF=∅.S_{F}=\emptyset. This is a contradiction again. Hence a>0a>0 as we have asserted.
